passage:
Monday: In the review, Jahnavi spoke fast. "What made you choose that? What was going through your head? Who approved it?" Sachin's chest went tight. He said, "It was in the brief," and stopped talking.
Tuesday: Sachin replied to every message with one word. He rehearsed his defence in the shower.
Wednesday: Jahnavi caught him at the coffee machine. "Yesterday my questions must have sounded like an attack. I'm sorry. Could you walk me through how the decision was made? I'd like to understand." Sachin looked up. "Sure. It began when the client changed the deadline, and I only had a day." Jahnavi nodded. "That helps. Thank you."

qa.q: What did Sachin say in the review after the fast questions?
What was Sachin feeling during the barrage of questions?
qa.a: Attacked and defensive. His chest went tight, and he stopped talking, then replied with one word for the day.

qa.q: What did Jahnavi change on Wednesday?
qa.a: Jahnavi apologised for how the questions sounded and asked Sachin to walk through how the decision was made, with genuine curiosity.

qa.q: How might Jahnavi have seen the first round of questions?
qa.a: As a way to understand a problem, without noticing how they sounded, until Jahnavi saw Sachin go quiet and reply with single words.

grounding: A person fired quick questions like why did you do that feels attacked; the same content asked with softer tone and curiosity gets better answers.

passage: Parul, I'm Binita, and I'll tell you about my first job at the newspaper. My editor, Mr Iqbal, would read my copy and bark, "Why did you write this? What were you thinking? Who told you that was a fact?" Every question felt like a slap. I stopped explaining. I just said, "Sorry," and my face went hot. Then I moved to another desk, under a woman called Sunita. Same mistake, same copy. She put it down and said, "Help me see how you got to this line?" I told her about my source, and even found the gap myself. The questions were nearly the same. The difference was in the voice. It stayed with me.

qa.q: What did Mr Iqbal bark at Binita's copy?
qa.a: "Why did you write this? What were you thinking? Who told you that was a fact?"

qa.q: What was Binita feeling when the editor asked the fast questions?
qa.a: Attacked and ashamed. Every question felt like a slap, so the face went hot and Binita only said sorry.

qa.q: What did Sunita do differently that helped Binita?
qa.a: Sunita put the copy down and asked calmly, "Help me see how you got to this line?", which invited an explanation.

qa.q: How might Sunita have seen Binita's mistake?
qa.a: As something to understand, since she asked how Binita got there, and was interested in the source and the reasoning.

grounding: A person fired quick questions feels attacked; the same content in a softer voice brings better answers.
